content: High-density lipoproteins (HDL) are a class of lipoproteins that vary in size, typically ranging from 8 to 11 nanometers in diameter. These particles are responsible for transporting cholesterol from peripheral tissues back to the liver, where it can either be excreted or reused. Approximately 30% of the cholesterol in the bloodstream is carried by HDL. HDL is hypothesized to play a role in removing cholesterol from atheromatous plaques within arteries and transporting it to the liver for disposal or recycling. This function is the primary reason HDL-bound cholesterol is often referred to as good cholesterol or HDL-C. Elevated levels of HDL-C are associated with a protective effect against cardiovascular diseases, whereas low levels of HDL cholesterol (less than 40 mg/dL in males and less than 50 mg/dL in females) are linked to an increased risk of heart disease. When cholesterol levels are measured, the cholesterol contained within HDL particles is considered beneficial for cardiovascular health, in contrast to the bad cholesterol carried by low-density lipoproteins (LDL). Most clinical trials aimed at preventing coronary artery disease (CAD) have focused on lowering LDL cholesterol levels using statins and other lipid-lowering drugs. These interventions have demonstrated improved clinical outcomes and reduced mortality. However, a direct causal relationship between low HDL cholesterol levels and the development of significant coronary artery disease has not been definitively established. Furthermore, there is insufficient evidence to confirm that raising HDL levels can reduce cardiovascular events in individuals with CAD. Statins are commonly used to treat patients with low HDL levels by targeting and reducing LDL cholesterol levels in the blood. HDL is considered good cholesterol because its levels are inversely proportional to the risk of coronary artery disease (CAD). In women, HDL levels above 60 mg/dL are regarded as a negative cardiac risk factor, meaning they are protective against heart disease. Epidemiological studies have demonstrated that high concentrations of HDL (greater than 60 mg/dL) provide protective benefits against cardiovascular diseases such as ischemic stroke and myocardial infarction. Conversely, low HDL concentrations (below 40 mg/dL in men and below 50 mg/dL in women) are considered a positive risk factor for atherosclerotic diseases. Data from the landmark Framingham Heart Study revealed that for a given LDL level, the risk of heart disease increases tenfold as HDL levels decrease from high to low. Similarly, for a fixed HDL level, the risk of heart disease increases threefold as LDL levels rise from low to high. Plasma HDL levels are inversely proportional to the development of coronary artery disease, making HDL a negative cardiac risk factor. Low serum HDL cholesterol can occur as an isolated abnormality or in association with hypercholesterolemia. Patients with premature coronary artery disease, defined as CAD occurring in men younger than 55 to 60 years and women younger than 65 years, often exhibit a primary reduction in HDL cholesterol levels. Studies have shown that the risk associated with low HDL levels is independent of the risk attributed to elevated LDL cholesterol levels in the serum. Findings from large-scale prospective studies indicate that for every 1 mg/dL increase in serum HDL levels, the risk of CAD decreases by approximately 2% in men and 3% in women. Although a causal relationship between low HDL-C levels and the incidence of coronary artery disease has not been definitively established, low HDL-C is considered a significant risk factor for CAD. Landmark clinical trials have been conducted to evaluate the effects of novel lipid-lowering agents on HDL-C levels and their impact on cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. For secondary prevention, statins and fibrates have proven effective in reducing cardiovascular risk in patients with low HDL levels compared to those with normal HDL levels. Fibrates are particularly effective when low HDL levels coincide with low LDL levels. Before considering combination therapy with statins and fibrates, dietary modifications and lifestyle changes should be implemented as effective strategies to raise HDL levels. However, combination therapy with statins and fibrates carries a risk of myopathy as a potential adverse effect. Future therapies show promise, including cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) inhibitors, which are currently in experimental phases. Combination therapy with statins and angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors is also considered a safe option for patients with low HDL levels who exhibit features of dysmetabolic syndrome. However, the preventive effects of these two drugs tend to be cumulative.
